title: MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
summary:
In Moldovan and Others v. Romania, the applicants were 25 Romanian nationals of Roma origin, all former residents of the village of Hădăreni in Mureş county. Represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, they brought their case against the Romanian state, highlighting the vulnerability of Roma and the severe harm they suffered due to racially motivated violence and the authorities’ failure to protect them. The case arose from events on 20 September 1993, when a conflict in Hădăreni escalated into a violent mob attack against the Roma community. Following the killing of a non-Roma villager, a crowd, including local police officers, set fire to the house where three Roma men were hiding, resulting in their deaths. The violence then spread, with villagers destroying Roma homes and property, while police failed to intervene. Many Roma families were left homeless, and the subsequent state response was inadequate, with only a few houses rebuilt and many families living in dire conditions for years.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court declared the case admissible, recognising the applicants’ claims as raising serious issues under the Convention. Although this 2003 decision concerned admissibility, it marked a crucial step in acknowledging the systemic discrimination and violence faced by Roma communities in Romania. The case is significant as it brought international attention to the persistent marginalisation of Roma and Travellers in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of anti-Roma violence and state inaction.
